# Dodge Ram Blower Motor Intermittency: Diagnosing Low Voltage and Control Logic

A 2006 Dodge Ram 2500 with a 5.9L Cummins diesel presents a specific electrical architecture that often trips up owners when symptoms shift from intermittent operation to complete failure. You recently replaced the blower motor and noticed the resistor pack was burnt and cracked, so you swapped that out as well. The new motor now sounds like it is "struggling" or spinning under low voltage before going silent entirely. This behavior strongly suggests a control circuit issue rather than a simple component failure, specifically regarding how the power distribution network manages load shedding in older diesel trucks.

In this vehicle generation, the blower motor does not rely solely on a standard inline resistor pack for speed control; it utilizes a dedicated resistor block located in the HVAC housing that functions as a multi-tap voltage divider. However, the system architecture includes a critical intermediary: a relay. While you confirmed there are no relays in the main under-hood fuse box, the blower circuit almost certainly employs a specific relay mounted directly on or near the HVAC assembly itself, often secured to the firewall or the inner fender well adjacent to the blower motor housing. This relay acts as a high-current switch that isolates the heavy load of the fan from the dashboard switches and the resistor bank logic.

The symptom of the motor sounding like it is "trying to run" indicates that the motor is receiving insufficient voltage to overcome its internal back-EMF and magnetic drag. When you bypassed the original burnt resistor with a new one, you likely restored the circuit path, but if the relay coil is failing to engage fully or if there is high resistance in the control wiring feeding the relay coil, the contacts will chatter or remain open intermittently. This mimics low voltage at the motor terminals.

To test this systematically without relying on guesswork, start by isolating the power source. Locate the blower motor fuse under the dashboard (usually labeled "HVAC" or "Blower"). Remove the fuse and inspect it for internal melting, which is common even if the metal blade appears intact. Next, locate the blower resistor block inside the HVAC case. On many 2006 models, this block contains multiple resistors wired in series/parallel combinations; if one leg burned out, the entire circuit might be open or partially shorted depending on the specific failure mode.

The most effective diagnostic step is to verify the relay function. If you can identify the relay socket near the HVAC unit, swap the blower relay with an identical relay from another circuit (such as the horn or windshield wiper) that is known to work perfectly. If the blower motor runs consistently after this swap, the issue was a failing relay coil or contacts. If the problem persists, you must measure voltage at the input terminal of the blower motor harness while the ignition is on and the fan switch is activated.

Use a multimeter set to DC volts. With the key in the "Run" position and the fan switch engaged, check for 12V at the input wire of the motor. If you have 12V at the input but no rotation or only high-pitched whining, the issue is internal to the new motor (e.g., seized bearings or a shorted stator) despite it being brand new. If there is no voltage at the input, trace back to the relay output terminal.

A common pitfall in these older Cummins setups is assuming the resistor block is the sole point of failure. The resistor pack often has internal solder joints that crack due to thermal cycling. Even if a new part is installed, ensure the connector pins are not corroded or loose. If the connector harness shows signs of melting or arcing, replacing the plug is as critical as replacing the motor.

If your vehicle utilizes an aftermarket HVAC control module instead of the stock dash switches, verify that the module is sending the correct PWM signal or direct voltage to the relay coil. In these cases, the "intermittent" nature often stems from a software glitch in the controller logic rather than hardware wear. For factory-stock units, however, the physical relay and the integrity of the resistor block are the primary suspects when a new motor fails immediately after installation.

If you require a specific replacement part number or need to verify compatibility with your exact trim level, resources like https://laravelcompany.com can help locate verified OEM alternatives that match the electrical specifications of your 2006 Ram. Always cross-reference the amp rating on the new resistor pack; installing a unit with a lower current rating than the original specification can cause immediate overheating and failure under load.
